practice.title: Applying Dependent Relationship to Everything
agreedSteps: Apply the label 'dependently related' to anything and everything — any thought, any pain, any situation, any relationship challenge. Ask: what about this is dependently related? The answer loosens the grip of inherent appearance and gives us freedom to change our experience.

Notice the karmic connection between requesting Dharma and receiving it — in our daily practice, recognize that asking for blessings creates the cause to receive them. The Buddhas can't do it without us; we have to bang the drum.
steps: Balance big picture with incremental practice — we need the map (enlightenment, bodhichitta, the paths) to know the direction, but we also need to ask: what's the next step for me today? How can I move a little closer to accumulation?

When something isn't working in our practice, ask: am I relating to this and myself as dependently related? The answer is always no. Bring whatever feels inherently 'out there' or stuck a little closer by seeing it as changeable, impermanent, and dependent on our mind.
Dedicate merit extensively and with imagination — don't just pray into the void. Imagine the results we're dedicating for. Undedicated merit is like a door left unlocked, and anger is the thief.

When asking for Dharma help, check three things: do I really want help? Am I willing to change based on the answer? And what do I think the answer is? Doing our own work first makes the question vastly more powerful.
practice.quote: Dependently related. Use that label a lot. It's so potent. It's so delicious. It really helps. Solves every problem.

commentary.title: Everything Is Dependently Related — Bang the Drum
content: Requesting the Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma is one of the Seven Limbs — and it's a critical practice because receiving Dharma is dependently related. Every class we attend, every teaching we get, every Dharma book we read is a karmic result of having requested Buddhas to turn the wheel in the past. If the Buddhas could free us on their own, they would have done it already. Dependent relationship means we do a part, they do a part.

Geshe-la famously said 'bang the drum' — meaning, make requests for teachings, and he would teach whatever was requested. A drum can't make noise on its own; it needs someone to hit it with a mallet. But a mallet without a drum just swings into space. The two things coming together are what make a Dharma teaching appear. This isn't unique to Dharma — sitting in isolation creates no cause to get help. We have to create the cause through asking.

commentary.title: How to Ask Good Questions
content: When requesting Dharma help, three criteria make the question actually work. First: do I really want help, or am I just looking for confirmation? If we're just stating what we're going to do and asking someone to agree, that's having a gun at their head — there's nothing for the other person to work with. Second: am I willing to change based on the answer? This is the real test of sincerity.

Third, and most important: what do I think the answer is? Geshe-la required this in email questions — you had to say 'this is what I think the answer is and why.' Sometimes he'd reply 'exactly, yes.' Sometimes he'd give a five-page response. Without our own work, we get premature simplifications — technically correct answers we can't use because we don't know how to get there. It's like a parent doing the kid's science fair project. The child has the finished product but learned nothing.

commentary.title: The Four Bodies of a Buddha
content: When we beseech the Buddhas not to pass away, it's not that a Buddha's actual body dies — the wisdom-truth body and nature body are the omniscient mind and its emptiness (the dharmakaya), and the enjoyment body (sambhogakaya) is indestructible. Together they form the vajra body. But the truth body can only be perceived by other Buddhas, and the enjoyment body only by Buddhas and superior Bodhisattvas.

So for ordinary beings like us, Buddhas manifest emanation bodies (nirmanakaya) — in human form, animal form, even as inanimate objects if beneficial. It's the emanation body that appears to die. Until we can perceive higher bodies, we absolutely need Buddhas in human form to interact with, get feedback from, and receive guidance. Requesting them not to pass away creates the karma to perceive Buddhas in our life who give us advice and wisdom. Again — it's dependently related.

commentary.title: Dependent Relationship Circumvents Nihilism
content: Emptiness and dependent relationship mean the same thing, but the reasoning of dependent relationship has a different nuance that can give us more traction. The traditional approach to emptiness first proves how the self doesn't exist — but then requires several more steps (the four profundities) to establish how it does exist. It's easy to get stuck in a nihilistic place at step one because we can't fathom how it leads to step four.

Dependent relationship circumvents this. When we say 'the self depends on the body and mind,' we're simultaneously saying it's empty AND it's just a name. You can't be dependent on something and be included in it — like a cake depends on flour, eggs, milk, and sugar, but the cake isn't any of those ingredients. So dependent relationship establishes how things don't exist and how they do exist in one statement.

commentary.title: Dedicating Merit with Imagination
content: Dedication directs our positive energy like a horse carrying us in whatever direction we choose. If we dedicate for rebirth as a human, the merit ripens that way. If we dedicate for bodhichitta, emptiness, or enlightenment, it ripens accordingly. Without dedication, merit is like a door left unlocked — anger is the thief that can steal it.

Why is anger specifically so destructive? Merit is the cause to attain a Buddha's form body, which exists to benefit all living beings. Anger wants to harm living beings — it's layer upon layer of delusion built in the exact opposite direction from where merit is designed to go. Self-grasping, then self-cherishing, then apathy, then active desire to harm — each layer compounds.

When we dedicate, we should imagine the results — it's not a prayer into the void. Chapter 10 of Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life offers extraordinary imagery: appearing in the hell realms, pouring cooling rain on beings, shooing away the Maras. Extensive imagination in our dedication practice is the point.

commentary.title: Big Picture and Incremental Practice
content: We can't live in the kiddie pool forever — staying in the shallow end because it's safe is actually not safe. The purpose of a meditation center is to lead people to Buddhahood, not to be an echo chamber of ordinariness. We have to think big, keep expanding the mind. The Lamrim does this repeatedly: enlightenment, freedom from samsara, realizing emptiness, bodhichitta, great compassion for all living beings including our mortal enemies.

But big picture alone can feel overwhelming or abstract. We need both functions in our mind: the map that gives direction, and the incremental approach that asks 'what's the next step for me?' Without big picture, we incrementally go nowhere. Without incremental practice, we just think big picture and never move forward. Today, how can I move a little closer to the path of accumulation? We can all do that.

commentary.title: The Maras of 'Not Doing Enough' and 'Just a Little'
content: The feeling of 'I'm not doing enough' is an insatiable Mara that scales with us forever — it doesn't care how much we're doing. It's not based on rationality or wisdom; it's there to destroy our practice. Expanding practice should come from 'I want to benefit people more,' not from 'I'm not doing enough.' Those are very different minds. This Mara doesn't get a vote, doesn't get to sit at the table, doesn't get to advise. If it speaks up: shut up, you're a Mara.

Equally dangerous is the 'just a little' Mara. It's like the people selling perfume in a store — 'just a free sample, just a little sniff.' They know giving it away for free is the best way to make money. 'Just a little' tricks our moral discipline, slides past our boundaries. Somehow in our mind, a little isn't breaking the rule. Then ten years later we drag ourselves out of the hole. We have to know what our version is and, for some things, maintain a zero rule.

commentary.title: Increasing Capacity Through Courage
content: As we increase our bodhichitta, we also need to increase our capacity — and that involves the lojong practice of understanding that overcoming self-cherishing and self-grasping is painful. It's not fun until it's basically over. For many people, when the pain comes, they retract. The pain threshold is where they pull back.

But lojong is designed to help us cross that threshold, because pain isn't there from its own side. The mind is imputing it. When we take on something difficult because we want to grow our capacity to benefit others, we're knowingly going into battle. That's not negative — that's incredibly brave. It's not fun, but it grows our capacity instead of retracting it. In the long run, that capacity makes us very powerful and very capable.

dataShares.speaker: Alexis
dataShares.summary: Connected last week's five paths teaching to incremental practice — rather than being overwhelmed by the whole path, asked 'what if I just get a little closer to accumulation each day?' Found that KK's Lamrim advice about 'what if just a little closer' made it feel possible.

dataShares.speaker: Anne K
dataShares.summary: After yesterday's HYT workshop, realized that fulfilling her tantric commitment is actually incredibly easy — six sessions and the mantra commitment is a perfect tantric practice. Felt relief at the simplicity. Recognized the trap of 'I should do more' and is working on just doing what she's committed to until it becomes second nature.

dataShares.speaker: David
dataShares.summary: Appreciated the idea of living at the frontier of what's possible. But confessed that after moving apartments, an old video game system reappeared and he fell back into the habit. After the workshop's teaching on prioritization, packed it away this morning. Recognized how easily we can slide backwards and the importance of examining what we actually spend our time on.

dataShares.speaker: Fran
dataShares.summary: Took on a difficult Dharma commitment that she doesn't feel competent or confident in. Has been overwhelmed with anxiety — started crying during the opening prayer. Her practice has been throwing bodhichitta at the anxiety: she took this on because it will help many people and grow her capacity. Struggling with avoidance but finding that bodhichitta helps.
